body.heading: A push from magnetism
paragraphs: An electric motor turns electrical energy into movement using a simple fact: a wire carrying current, placed in a magnetic field, feels a force. Put many turns of wire on a rotor between magnets, and those small pushes add up to a steady turning force called torque.

The trick is keeping the push in the same rotational direction. As the rotor turns, the current in its coils must be reversed at the right moment, again and again, so the force always pushes the rotor onwards instead of back.

body.heading: Switching the current
paragraphs: In a simple direct-current motor, a split ring called a commutator does the switching mechanically, flipping the current each half-turn as brushes slide over it. Larger motors for electric cars use electronics instead, switching the current in stationary coils with split-second timing.

Either way, the result is the same: magnetic fields chase each other around in a circle, and the rotor follows. Speed is controlled by changing the voltage or the switching rate — no gears or clutch are needed for the motor itself to start turning.

body.heading: Quiet, instant strength
paragraphs: Electric motors are efficient — a good one turns 85 percent or more of its electrical energy into motion, wasting far less as heat than a fuel engine. They also deliver their strongest turning force from a standstill, which is why electric cars pull away so sharply.

The same design, scaled down, spins cooling fans, washing machines and hard drives; scaled up, it drives trains and factory machinery. One principle — current in a magnetic field feels a force — covers nearly all of them.

description: Pass current through a coil inside a magnetic field and the coil is pushed — arrange it well and it spins.
